title: 1,100 Hours and 400 Shifts: Joe Palomino Kept Showing Up for Hungry East Texans
summary: Joe Palomino has volunteered more than 1,100 hours across 400 shifts at the East Texas Food Bank's Texarkana Resource Center. His service began with a simple offer to help during the center's first parking-lot distribution.
content:
Joe Palomino did not wait for a formal invitation when the East Texas Food Bank began distributing food from the parking lot of its unfinished Texarkana Resource Center in 2024. He saw the work, asked whether he could help and kept returning.

By the time the food bank presented its 2025 Hunger Hero Awards this month, Palomino had logged more than 1,100 volunteer hours across 400 shifts. The organization named him its Volunteer Hunger Hero, recognizing a pattern of service measured not by one dramatic moment but by hundreds of reliable appearances.

The distinction matters in hunger relief. Food has to be received, sorted, packed, moved and distributed on schedule. Families need to know a pantry or resource center will be open when promised. A volunteer who returns week after week becomes part of the infrastructure that makes that promise possible.

The food bank says Palomino has supported the Texarkana center since its opening period, helping with food distributions, sorting projects and daily tasks. Its award announcement describes him as someone whose consistency and willingness to help strengthened the operation as the new location took shape.

## A regional need behind one volunteer's record

The East Texas Food Bank serves 26 counties covering about 20,000 square miles. It works with more than 200 partner pantries and feeding programs, and its published fiscal-year facts say it provided 30 million meals and served 153,800 households in fiscal 2026.

The organization estimates that 232,940 people in its service area face hunger, including 83,090 children. Put another way, its current materials describe food insecurity as affecting about one in six East Texans and one in four children. Those are modeled regional estimates, not a count of every person who visits a pantry, but they explain why dependable local capacity matters.

Texarkana sits at the northeastern edge of the food bank's Texas service area. A resource center there shortens the distance between regional supply and Bowie County families, while also supporting partner organizations. Volunteers extend the paid staff's reach, particularly during distribution days when traffic, lifting, packing and client assistance happen at the same time.

Palomino's 1,100 hours are equivalent to more than 27 standard 40-hour workweeks. The 400-shift total also shows that the contribution was distributed over time. That durability is what makes the story useful: generosity is not limited to a large check or a single emergency. Repeated, ordinary work can add up to exceptional public value.

## Other East Texans honored

The seventh annual awards recognized a wider network of service. Church on the Rock in Texarkana received the Partner Agency Hunger Hero award after operating an emergency pantry for more than a decade and distributing the equivalent of more than 58,000 meals, according to the food bank.

The SWEPCO Foundation received the Corporate Hunger Hero award. The food bank credits its support with helping provide more than 2.1 million meals through East Texas programs. Marvin Methodist Church in Tyler was named Faith-Based Hunger Hero; the organization says the church has supported its work since 1988 and helped provide more than 872,000 meals.

The Individual Hunger Hero honor was awarded posthumously to Lauren Hogan. The food bank says Hogan volunteered alongside her father, Mike, while living with stage 4 colon cancer. She died in September 2025 at age 38, and her father continues to volunteer weekly. Her recognition places courage and service together without turning illness into spectacle.

KLTV also reported on the awards and the honorees, providing independent local confirmation of the food bank's announcement. The underlying service totals come from the East Texas Food Bank, which is the organization maintaining the volunteer and meal records.

## How to turn admiration into help

The practical response to a volunteer story is not merely applause. The food bank lists opportunities for individuals and groups to sort food, pack boxes and assist at distributions. Because needs and age requirements can vary by site and shift, prospective volunteers should use the organization's current volunteer calendar rather than arriving without notice.

People who need food can use the food bank's pantry locator and program pages to find nearby assistance. Available hours, eligibility steps and inventory can change, so contacting the listed partner before traveling is sensible. The organization also operates benefits-assistance and nutrition programs in addition to distributing food through partner agencies.

Donors should evaluate the same things they would for any nonprofit: audited financial statements, program results, governance and how restricted gifts are used. The food bank publishes organizational information and an annual impact report. Transparency does not diminish charity; it helps supporters understand what their time and money accomplish.

Palomino's story is especially strong because it does not depend on an invented rescue or a staged photograph. The documented accomplishment is the accumulation itself: more than 1,100 hours, 400 shifts and a decision to keep returning after that first parking-lot distribution.

RepWatchr's accompanying image is an original symbolic illustration of anonymous food-bank volunteers. It is not a photograph of Palomino, the Texarkana center or a specific distribution, and it does not attempt to recreate his likeness.

East Texas communities often rely on people whose names never appear in a headline. This time, the record is public. Joe Palomino saw a new operation that needed hands, offered his own and stayed long enough to become one of the people others could count on. That is what a community hero looks like in the ledger: one shift, then another, until service becomes a landmark.
